chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, who said:

I witnessed Ibn Abi Layth judging in the case of a man who had assigned the yield of his house to one of his relatives and did not stipulate a time period. So the man died, and his inheritors came to Ibn Abi Layth, and the relative to whom the house was assigned also came. So Ibn Abi Layth said, 'I view that it should be left as its owner had left it.'

Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Thaqafi said to him, 'Indeed, Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) had judged in this mosque contrary to what you have judged.' He said, 'And what is your knowledge (of this)?' He said, 'I heard Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him) saying: The Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) judged for the return of the withheld (assets) and the enforcement of the inheritance.'

Ibn Abi Layth said, 'Is this with you in a book?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'So send for it and bring it to me.' Muhammad ibn Muslim said to him, 'On the condition that you do not look into the book except in that specific hadith.' He said, 'That is up to you.'
So he showed him the hadith from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) in the book, so he retracted his judgement.
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali (peace be upon him) rule on lifetime endowments without specified duration?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential tension between the Hanafi judge Ibn Abi Layth’s view of indefinite lifetime endowments and the Shia Imams’ ruling that such assets revert to the general inheritance pool upon the donor's death. Muhammad ibn Muslim’s successful challenge, based on the precedent of Imam Ali (AS) and Imam al-Baqir (AS), establishes the principle that unspecified duration gifts are treated as temporary usufructs rather than permanent transfers, ensuring heirs receive their rightful shares. This case underscores the Shia emphasis on strict adherence to prophetic and imamic legal precedents over local judicial customs.
